passage.title: Ancient DNA and the Rewriting of Human History

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of its short history, the field of palaeogenomics — the study of genetic material recovered from ancient remains — was effectively confined to cold places. Low temperatures slow the chemical processes that destroy DNA after death, so the best-preserved samples tended to come from permafrost, northern caves and high-altitude sites. Warmer regions such as Africa and Southeast Asia, despite their rich fossil deposits, were widely assumed to be genetic graveyards in which no usable DNA could survive for long. A series of studies published in recent months has overturned this assumption, pushed the recovery of ancient DNA deeper into the past, and forced archaeologists to rethink long-established narratives about how human populations moved, mixed and adapted.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A striking example comes from South Africa. Writing in Quaternary Science Reviews, an international team led by Deon de Jager screened 144 fossil teeth and bones drawn from 320 specimens collected at six cave and rock-shelter sites along the country's southern coast. The material spanned roughly 110,000 years and belonged to six species of wild bovids — the mammal family that includes antelope and buffalo. Ancient DNA was successfully recovered from 65 of the samples, a success rate of 45 percent, and one tooth from a mountain reedbuck yielded genetic material estimated to be around 50,000 years old, the oldest yet retrieved from sub-Saharan Africa. Before this study, the record holder was a 9,300-year-old extinct blue antelope.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The key to this result lay as much in the laboratory as in the fossils. The team compared a conventional method that targets intact double-stranded DNA with a newer single-stranded approach, which effectively unzips damaged molecules and recovers tiny fragments that standard protocols miss. Using the newer technique, they obtained up to 6.7 times more animal DNA. Even so, the authors remain cautious: the reedbuck sample had been contaminated with human DNA, although this was corrected, and they recommend that future projects concentrate on Holocene specimens, which consistently yielded the highest recovery rates. The success suggests that warm-climate preservation is less hopeless than once believed, but it also exposes the fragility of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Palaeogenomics is also redrawing the map of East Asian prehistory. In Science Advances, a team including Guanglin He reported a resource of more than 1,000 newly sequenced Y chromosomes from previously underrepresented groups. Their time-calibrated family tree traces early paternal lineages back to the Paleolithic, pointing to migrations out of the southern Himalayas, followed by Neolithic expansions linked to the spread of millet and rice farming. The data reveal both inland and coastal routes connecting South China with Southeast Asia, and suggest that distinct hunter-gatherer and farming groups, including the ancestors of Tibeto-Burman speakers, moved south in successive waves. These later movements appear to have shaped the paternal landscape observed in the region today.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A companion study in the same journal examined the consequences of those movements. By analysing 1,507 high-coverage Y-chromosome sequences from China alongside 780 ancient genomes and 1,748 low-coverage sequences from Southeast Asia, researchers reconstructed a high-resolution phylogeny that points to repeated, male-biased expansions out of Neolithic South China. Founding lineages associated with Hmong-Mien and Tai-Kadai speakers grew markedly during the Middle Neolithic, and their descendants remain prominent in the paternal ancestry of South China and mainland Southeast Asia. The picture that emerges is not one of a single migration, but of recurrent waves that together built the region's genetic landscape.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: These genetic findings sometimes clash with long-standing archaeological assumptions. A team led by Wang Chuanchao of Fudan University recovered 112 high-quality genomes from eight sites in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, spanning more than 6,200 years of continuous ancestry traceable to the Yangshao culture. Contrary to what written records suggest, the researchers detected no significant genetic contribution from steppe nomadic groups to the main population of the Central Plains. Wang argues that the entry of nomadic peoples was reflected mainly in political and cultural integration, with incoming groups rapidly assimilated into a much larger local population. The result challenges migration-based explanations for cultural change.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The broader picture of human origins is becoming more tangled as well. Most non-Africans carry roughly two percent Neanderthal DNA, although the proportion varies — about 2.3 percent in East Asians and 1.8 percent in Europeans — and Denisovan ancestry reaches four to six percent in island Southeast Asia and Oceania. Using a computational method called TRACE on 503 present-day genomes, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley identified a 'ghost' lineage that diverged from the ancestors of modern humans around 800,000 years ago and still contributes up to one percent of every human genome, with a second, older lineage entering through the Denisovans. Human evolution resembles a braided network rather than a branching tree.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: With such power comes responsibility, and the field has had to confront its own record. A 2017 study of ancient DNA from Chaco Canyon in New Mexico was criticised for referring to a tribal ancestor as 'cranium 14' and for failing to consult local communities. In response, an international group of 64 researchers from 31 countries published guidelines in Nature urging colleagues to follow local regulations, plan carefully, minimise damage to bones, make data available for re-examination and engage with all stakeholders. Even this effort drew criticism: Indigenous geneticists such as Nanibaa' Garrison and Krystal Tsosie argued that the guidelines did not go far enough on consent and data sovereignty. The debate underlines that studying ancient lives now depends as much on trust as on technology.
